title: Mohini pours the nectar
hookLine: the nectar's out, the asuras grab, and Mohini pours it as a gift
carry: amrita is poured as grace, not grabbed
tomorrow: the earth itself sinks into the sea. who goes down for it?
last: BOTH READINGS AGREE ON THE ORDER.

cards: The first spoonful of something sweet after a long, hard day: people slow down for it. The pot of amrita is out of the sea, carried by Dhanvantari, and the moment it appears, the asuras grab it.
They pulled half the rope; they want it all. The gods can't win it back by force. Then a woman walks into the middle of the quarrel, so lovely that everyone stops arguing.

teach.b: She's Mohini, Vishnu in a new form. In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, the asuras hand her the pot themselves and ask her to share it out. She seats the two sides in rows and pours for the gods.
One asura, Rahu, slips into the gods' row in disguise and gets a sip. The Sun and the Moon call him out, and Vishnu's discus takes his head.
But the nectar has already touched his mouth, so the head lives on; some tellings say that's why, now and then, Rahu swallows the Sun or the Moon: an eclipse. Now the line the Bhagavata doesn't hide.

Gods and asuras did the same work, in the same place, on the same rope, and the results weren't the same. The text puts the difference down to one thing: the gods took refuge in Vishnu. The nectar wasn't a wage.
It was poured. That's the heart of bhakti, devotion: what matters most comes as grace, received, not grabbed.
And you can taste it at the end of a puja, when someone pours a spoonful of panchamrit, the five nectars of milk, curd, ghee, honey and sugar, into your cupped right palm.
You don't reach for it. You hold out your hand, and you sip.

how: At the end of many pujas, panchamrit is poured into the cupped right palm and sipped as prasad; the story of Mohini and the amrita is retold from the Bhagavata Purana, and in some places Rahu is named in traditional explanations of eclipses.

o: Vishnu's lovely form who pours the nectar for the gods
the pot of nectar Dhanvantari carries up from the sea
the tortoise who held the churning until the nectar came

p: Vishnu's form who shares the nectar
sneaks a sip in the gods' row

s: Mohini is a separate goddess, not Vishnu
in the Bhagavata, Mohini is Vishnu in a new form.
the asuras hand Mohini the pot themselves
they ask her to share it out, and she pours for the gods.
the gods won the nectar because they worked harder
in the Bhagavata the work was the same on both sides; the difference was refuge in Vishnu.

games.q: after puja, your aunt is pouring panchamrit into everyone's palm. your little cousin grabs the spoon to serve himself. by the churning, what's off?
o: it's given, not taken: you hold out your hand and receive it.
nothing; it's the same panchamrit either way.
he should wait until the adults have eaten first.
games.why: the asuras grabbed the pot; Mohini poured. in bhakti what matters most comes as grace, so prasad is received in an open palm.

practice: If you have water or anything small to eat, first set it in front of you for a moment, the way Hindus offer food to God before eating so it comes back as prasad. Then take one sip or one bite and don't swallow right away.
Let it sit on your tongue: the temperature, the taste, what changes as you wait. Then swallow, and notice what stays. If you don't pray, let it simply be a gift you didn't make.

wordCard.voice: Kurma: the tortoise who held the mountain so the nectar could come up at last.

orig.note: Sanskrit amrita: the nectar the whole churning was for.

carryVoice: Hold onto this one: amrita is poured as grace, not grabbed. Hold out your hand. Rest well.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.8–8.9 (the asuras seize the amrita; Mohini; Rahu in the gods' row; the Sun and Moon; the discus; equal effort, different results)
